frameworks.name: $100 Million Scaling Roadmap
frameworks.definition: A 10-stage growth framework that identifies where businesses get stuck and prescribes functional strategies (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance) at each stage.

frameworks.name: Identity-Action Loop
frameworks.definition: The mechanism that identity follows from repeated action, not vice versa; what you do publicly becomes how others describe you, making identity 100% controllable through deliberate behavioral choices.

claims.text: Self-limiting identity statements ("I'm not good at math", "I'm not techie") sabotage goal achievement by filtering out actions and people that contradict the claimed identity. The test for any belief is: does this increase or decrease the likelihood I hit my goals?
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when the belief reduces options consistent with goal-seeking
claims.mechanism: Self-limiting identity statements constrain the set of actions a person considers available, eliminating paths to goal achievement.
bounded_by: Not about positive delusions or false confidence
The test is empirical (does it help hit goals), not emotional (does it feel good)

claims.text: Identity is not fixed by childhood events or prior setbacks. Alex Hormozi considered himself bad at math after a poor algebra teacher in 9th grade set him back, but in his 20s chose to reframe: he identified the skill he wanted (rapid mental arithmetic), practiced without a calculator for years, and now is described by others as strong at math. Mechanism: the identity follows the repeated action, not the reverse.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when identity was formed by single negative event
when the person has capacity to practice the contradicting skill
claims.mechanism: Identity is retroactively assigned by observers based on repeated public action, not pre-determined by earlier setbacks. Changing action changes the identity others assign.
bounded_by: Requires years of deliberate practice, not a one-time action
Works for skills and behaviors, not inherent capacities

claims.text: Doing is being. People's names and descriptions have always been derived from their actions ("John the Carpenter", "John the Stonesmith"); the first question when meeting someone is "What do you do?", and identity is 100% under control because it flows entirely from what a person chooses to do.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when describing who someone is to others
over a time horizon where repeated action is observable
bounded_by: Identity is not about internal feeling or belief, only external action
Only applies retrospectively—identity is assigned after action is demonstrated

claims.text: Childhood difficulty does not determine present capability. Everyone has had a difficult childhood; the relevant fact is what actions you take now to hit your goals. Past hardship is not a limiting factor—only present choices are.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Not claiming childhood has no developmental impact
Only that past hardship is not a valid constraint on future action

claims.text: People are far more changeable than they believe. A single bad teacher or setback early in life can create a false identity ("I'm bad at X") that persists for years, but the pliability to change that identity is always present—the constraint is choice, not capability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when the limiting belief was formed by a single event or period

claims.text: The $100 Million Scaling Roadmap breaks business growth into 10 predictable stages and identifies the functional constraints (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance) that block progress at each stage. This is derived from analyzing Acquisition.com portfolio companies and where they got stuck and how they escaped.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: for B2B and service-based businesses in the Acquisition.com cohort

examples.text: Alex Hormozi believed he was bad at math after failing to learn algebra properly in 9th grade due to a poor teacher. The setback put him back a year academically, and he carried the identity "I'm just not good at math" into his 20s. In his 20s, he decided this identity no longer served his goals. He observed that people who could do mental arithmetic seemed competent, so he committed to not using a calculator for anything. He made mistakes initially but improved through repeated practice. He checked his work against a calculator after completing calculations to verify. Over years of this practice, the identity shifted: people now describe him as someone who "rattles off numbers like crazy." The mechanism is not that he suddenly became "naturally" good at math, but that his repeated public action (mental arithmetic) changed how others described him, which eventually became his own identity.

Hormozi observes that children's names historically were occupational: John the Carpenter, John the Stonesmith, John the Mason. Modern naming conventions have changed, but the underlying principle persists—when you meet someone, the first question is "What do you do?" and people describe others by their actions. This shows that identity has always been derived from doing, not from inherent characteristics, making identity fully controllable through choice of action.

practices.text: Run every belief, action, person, and circumstance through the filter: does this increase or decrease the likelihood I hit my goals? Use this filter to eliminate beliefs and people that don't serve goal achievement.

If you want to change an aspect of your identity, identify the skill or behavior you want to be known for, and commit to repeated public practice of that behavior until others start to describe you that way.

Visit acquisition.com/roadmap, enter your business information, and identify which of the 10 scaling stages your business is at. Use the framework's functional guidance (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance) to diagnose what to do next.
